name: Adam Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 43, and I lead an electrical crew doing homes and business repairs. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the firm's strongest people on a difficult fault. This morning I worked out why a workshop circuit only failed after lunch, then checked the crew's test results before the handover. I like explaining the actual cause to a customer; I dislike being halfway through a proper explanation when the next booking starts ringing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household position, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner plans delivery routes for a supplier, and our children are nine and fifteen. We have a mortgage, twelve months of normal expenses saved, high pay from my job and plenty of electrical firms nearby. I use AI occasionally for draft customer notes after a colleague has shown the tool works, checking against the actual job. I prefer a small proven improvement to taking a side in a grand argument; our ordinary household budget still uses both wages.

say: I'd keep a **useful draft note** without making every improvement into a new way of living.
I'd retain **clear test explanations** so customers understood the actual repair.
think: Our **two wages** and year-long reserve make household work and money feel secure in this mild picture.
A small note-writing improvement can help without needing to become a **replacement job** for someone.
do: Continue leading **repairs** and checking occasional customer-note drafts through the first plateau year.
Keep the **family budget** and existing paid test and explanation time rather than buy unnecessary subscriptions.
feel: **Calm** about work and household living, with room to enjoy ordinary repairs and family evenings.
S0.quote: A better sentence is useful only if the customer gets a better account of the work.
fieldNote: His **calm** rests on two continuing wages, high trade pay, many local employers and substantial savings, not on a tool's promise.
His **occasional checked notes** remain routine, while held cash doesn't become new saving simply because the scenario stays mild.

steps.text: Continue leading repairs, checking occasional notes and retaining paid tests and explanations

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful draft note could stay useful without becoming a whole new trade. I'd still want a customer to understand the test result and the repair. We don't have to make every small improvement sound like a new way of living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both wages and our household money feel secure in that picture. The reserve gives us time if an ordinary bill or a quiet month arrives. I can enjoy a little less writing without needing it to replace somebody's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep leading the repairs and checking the occasional drafted notes. Through the first plateau year I'd keep the normal family budget and the paid time we already use for tests and explanations. I'd buy no extra subscription just to keep a story about progress going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and living, and glad not every week needs a new plan. I'd still enjoy getting a stubborn fault right. I'd be happy to get home and talk about the children's day instead of the next product launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the drafted note helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the checked result and actual time it took, including corrections. I don't mind a plain note if it's true. A better sentence is useful only if the customer gets a better account of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the existing reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it available for real trouble rather than spend it because a forecast sounded reassuring. It's already saved money, not a new deposit made by the scenario. I wouldn't treat a year of expenses as permission to stop earning.

say: I'd recognise **route planning** as exposed thinking work rather than celebrate faster plans without discussing paid hours.
I'd keep **practical repairs** and an occasional useful note tool in their proper place within the household picture.
think: My repair wage may hold while my partner loses **route-planning hours**.
A **year's reserve** protects the next payment without making a household wage reduction unimportant.
do: End the **garden-maintenance plan** only with partner agreement and shared basic garden work.
Keep **paid repairs** and review both actual wages monthly during the first year, protecting children's essentials and the reserve.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household income loss, while confident the next mortgage payment is covered.
S1.quote: Being comfortable about next month's mortgage isn't the same as being unworried about losing part of a wage.
fieldNote: His **household anxiety** follows real exposure in the partner's planning tasks, while his own practical wage and substantial reserve remain resources.
The **spending cut** requires consent and shared labour, without inventing extra saving or assigning his partner an unchosen career.

steps.text: End paid garden maintenance only with partner agreement and shared basic garden work
Keep repairs and review actual wages monthly, protecting children’s essentials and the reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the planning on that card sounds much like the work my partner does. I'd want to hear what paid hours the supplier actually expected to retain, not just celebrate quicker routes. I'd keep my own practical work and the note tool in perspective.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair wage should hold for now, but my partner's route-planning hours could shrink. We'd feel that in our household income even with a year's reserve. Being comfortable about next month's mortgage isn't the same as being unworried about losing part of a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my partner to compare actual paid hours and receipts with our monthly budget, without claiming I could choose the next job for someone else. We'd end the paid garden-maintenance plan only with agreement between us and share the basic garden work. In the first year I'd keep the repairs and review both actual wages monthly, protecting the children's essentials and the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household income, not frightened of the next mortgage payment. I'd feel a bit awkward praising a useful note tool while my partner worried about route planning being bought more cheaply. Both feelings would be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would do the garden work after cancelling the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my share rather than announce the cut and leave the extra work to my partner. We'd keep the basic garden manageable instead of trying to match a paid service's standard. It would reduce spending, not prove we'd increased saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your partner to retrain immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what the actual employer plan said and what my partner wanted to check. A course title or a friend's story wouldn't be a chosen new job. I'd want the household to use real terms rather than my confident guesses.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning work** from robots around 2031 and explain that household wages face different dates.
I'd retain **paid repairs** while asking what later physical competition means for my own hours.
think: I expect a **large planning-wage loss** for my partner in 2028.
A **year's reserve** gives choices without guaranteeing how quickly either adult can find dependable earnings after later changes.
do: End **paid garden maintenance** only with partner agreement and shared work, protecting children's essentials and the reserve.
Request **free community advice**, checking availability and eligibility without assuming an appointment.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and count no support or payment relief before approval.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected major household income loss, with night-time sums despite a reserve and deliberate actions.
S2.quote: I wouldn't call an unanswered request an appointment already in the diary.
fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected major partner-income loss and sleep disruption, while the cash buffer gives control rather than erasing the worry.
The **advice request** stays unconfirmed, support requires approval, and no investment return or alternative job is invented to close the household gap.

steps.text: End paid garden maintenance only with partner agreement and shared basic garden work

Keep paid repairs after 2028; count no support or payment relief before approval
Protect children's essentials and retain the twelve-month cash reserve while cutting adult spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. The route-planning wage at home wouldn't get the physical trade's extra time. I'd still keep paid repair work while asking what the later stage meant for my own hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large part of my partner's planning wage to go when thinking work became that capable and cheap. My own wage might hold longer, but robots could later squeeze it too. I'd lose sleep over how long two adults might need to find a dependable earning arrangement, even with a year put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd end the garden plan only by agreement and share the basic work, without touching children's essentials or the reserve. I'd request free community budget advice, checking availability and eligibility rather than assuming an appointment or payment. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and budget from actual agreed wages, counting no support or payment relief before approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large household loss, with enough money to make deliberate choices rather than panic. I'd still be able to pick up the phone and ask. That wouldn't stop me repeating the sums at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the community advice service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wage records, actual essential bills and mortgage terms, and ask what help could really be checked. If the advice wasn't available, I'd ask where else offered free community help. I wouldn't call an unanswered request an appointment already in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for an investment to replace the threatened wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't try to make the expected wage gap disappear in an investment forecast. The reserve would stay available for the household. I'd count what we had and what employers had actually agreed to pay.

say: I'd use **five years** for checked household choices while keeping the thinking and robot dates separate.
I wouldn't call **extra preparation** the same thing as another employer agreeing to pay a wage.
think: I still expect a **large planning-wage loss** in 2031 without a confirmed replacement.
The **later wage gap** keeps me awake, despite more time and a full year's cash buffer.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and review actual household money monthly.
Buy **100 monthly** in a share fund including fees, only from wage surplus after essentials; the investment could lose value.
Keep the **twelve-month cash reserve** untouched, require continuing partner agreement and stop purchases if either wage falls.
feel: **Alarmed** about the wage gap, while making a small separate investment without assuming it replaces income.
S3.quote: I wouldn't count a hoped-for gain as money for the next mortgage payment.
fieldNote: His **investment choice** remains separate from the feared wage gap, with possible losses acknowledged and no return assumed for mortgage payments.
The **cash protections** preserve a full year's reserve, spare-wage funding, included fees and continuing partner consent, stopping purchases after either wage falls.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs and review actual household money monthly after 2031
Buy 100 monthly of a share fund, including fees, only from wages left after essentials
Keep twelve-month cash reserve untouched; buy only with continuing partner agreement, stopping if either wage falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a household do more than make one hurried choice. I'd still keep the 2031 thinking date and robots around 2034 separate. I wouldn't call extra preparation the same as another agreed wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large planning-wage loss in 2031 without a confirmed replacement, and that keeps me awake. More time helps us compare actual choices, but it doesn't remove the later income need. I'd still be only 51 when the robots followed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the repair wage and review actual household money monthly. With continuing partner agreement, I'd buy 100 monthly in a share fund, which owns small pieces of many companies, including all fees within the 100 and using only wage surplus after essentials. I'd leave the twelve-month cash reserve untouched, stop purchases if either wage fell, and keep those conditions in the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the future wage gap, but able to make a small separate long-term choice. I'd be ready for the fund to fall in value. I wouldn't count a hoped-for gain as money for the next mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You expect a wage loss; why make an investment at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The investment would be a small amount from money genuinely left after bills, not a plan to replace the lost wage. We'd keep a full year in cash and stop buying if either wage fell or agreement ended. I can worry and still make a limited choice without claiming it's the rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the monthly fund purchase?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 100 would include fees, not sit on top of them. If there wasn't 100 spare after essentials, there wouldn't be a purchase. I'd want the provider's actual charges clear before starting, and I'd accept that the investment itself could lose money.

say: I'd use **ten years** for several decisions rather than choose the children's whole future from a card.
I'd seek **written paid hours** for adults while helping the children examine real learning offers when choices arise.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume pensions, adult children's income or a cleared mortgage.
My practical wage looks secure near term, but **planning tools** could cut the other household wage earlier.
do: Keep **paid repairs** and review actual household money monthly.
Buy **100 monthly** in a share fund including fees, only from wage surplus after essentials; the fund can lose value.
Preserve the **twelve-month cash reserve**, require continuing partner agreement and stop purchases if either wage falls.
feel: **Anxious** about possible earlier household wage loss, with less urgency about the distant full change.
S4.quote: A full cash reserve wouldn't make my family's share-fund purchases my decision alone.
fieldNote: He **ages both children** before discussing their choices, counting neither future child earnings nor an assumed pension as household income.
His **investment limits** persist over the longer horizon, including continuing consent, spare-wage funding, included fees and an untouched cash reserve.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs and review actual household money monthly after 2036
Buy 100 monthly of a share fund, including fees, only from wages left after essentials
Keep twelve-month cash reserve untouched; buy only with continuing partner agreement, stopping if either wage falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets us make several decisions without picking the children's whole future from one card. I'd help them check real learning offers when they had an actual choice. I'd still want written paid hours from the adults' employers, not only promises about future skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when robots followed; the children would be nineteen and twenty-five in 2036. I couldn't assume pensions, their earnings or a cleared mortgage. My own practical wage looks secure for the next few years, but planning tools could cut my partner's hours sooner, so the household income still worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid repairs and review actual household money monthly. I'd use the same 100 share-fund purchase only from wage surplus after essentials, including fees within the 100, with continuing partner agreement and the twelve-month cash reserve untouched. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep those limits and stop purchases if either wage fell, counting no investment gain as a replacement wage. The fund could still lose value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible earlier household income loss, with less pressure from the distant full change. I'd have time to inspect an actual opportunity before choosing it. I wouldn't turn the children being adults later into a pension for me now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your partner wanted to stop the investments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop, because agreement would be a continuing condition rather than permission I'd collected once. A full cash reserve wouldn't make my family's share-fund purchases my decision alone. I'd also stop if bills used up the spare wage money, even if neither wage had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer picture change plans for the children today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't decide their studies from this card or include their possible wages in our budget. I'd tell them to read the actual work, fees and paid time before choosing. I'd rather show them how to ask than pretend their father knew the safe answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the planning wage to be hit before we have another agreed source of income. Honest written paid hours and accessible community advice using our actual figures would help. A year's reserve gives us time to choose, not a second signature on a wage agreement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone's investment plan is really being used to hide a missing wage in the sums. Mine can't replace the planning income, and the fund can lose money. I'd want that written as plainly as the fact that I can afford a small trial.

headlineQuote: A year's reserve gives us time to choose, not a second signature on a wage agreement.
portrait: **Adam, 43**, leads electrical crews with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence.
His **high trade pay**, twelve-month reserve and many local employers support a household with partner, two schoolchildren and mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally after proof**, while the partner's delivery-route planning faces earlier thinking-work risks than his own practical repairs.
Expected **planning-wage losses** alarm him in the faster pictures; small investments use only fee-inclusive spare wages and never count as replacement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut the planning wage before the household has another agreed earning source.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **written paid hours** would clarify actual wages.
Accessible **community advice** using actual household figures would help compare choices without assuming assistance.
